sections.title: Introduction — Readiness Without Panic
sections.html:
Introduction — Readiness Without Panic

The survey team has entered the building. A nurse is searching for a treatment record. A department head wants to know what to say. The Administrator is receiving document requests. At the same time, residents still need medications, meals, transfers, toileting, assessment, reassurance, and ordinary human attention. This is the moment when a facility discovers whether survey readiness was a project or a system.

Panic begins when readiness depends on memory, heroics, and a few people who know where everything is. Control begins when leaders can see risk, staff understand the work, records reflect reality, corrections are verified, and requests move through a practiced process. The purpose of this book is to build that control without turning the facility into a permanent mock survey.

What This Book Promises

By the end, a DON should be able to identify the building's highest-risk systems, conduct focused resident tracers, prepare staff through competency rather than scripting, recognize serious-warning conditions, build systemic correction, write an operational Plan of Correction, assemble credible evidence, lead survey-day coordination, and sustain readiness through QAPI.

How to Use the System

Read Parts I and II to create a resident-centered readiness method.

Use Parts III and IV when correcting findings or building a Plan of Correction.

Use Part V to rehearse survey operations before the team arrives.

Complete the field tools with the interdisciplinary team; do not make them nursing-only paperwork.

Replace examples with current federal, state, local, and facility-specific requirements.

The Readiness Cycle

See

Protect

Understand

Correct

Verify

Observe risk and contradictions

Address immediate resident exposure

Find scope and causes

Change resident and system conditions

Test implementation and durability

This cycle repeats. Verification may reveal a new weakness, which becomes the next problem to understand. That is not failure; it is how a learning system works.

sections.title: PART I — SEE THE BUILDING CLEARLY
sections.html:
PART I — SEE THE BUILDING CLEARLY

1. See the Building Before the Surveyor Does

A survey does not create a building's weaknesses. It reveals weaknesses that were already present, often in plain sight but separated across shifts, departments, and records. The survey-ready DON learns to see those fragments as one operating system.

Readiness Is a Daily Management Practice

Survey readiness is not a binder, a mock-survey week, or a polished tour route. It is the ability to show that residents receive required care every day; staff understand their responsibilities; leaders recognize breakdowns; and correction continues until it is effective. A facility can have attractive policies and still be vulnerable when practice, resident experience, and documentation disagree. The DON's first responsibility is therefore visibility: knowing where the greatest resident harm could occur and whether the controls are actually working.

Build a Risk Picture

Start with information that describes the building as residents experience it: new and worsening wounds, falls with injury, unexplained weight change, avoidable hospital transfers, infections, allegations, elopement risk, medication errors, dialysis coordination, changes in condition, grievances, call-offs, and competency gaps. Add prior deficiencies, complaint themes, facility-reported incidents, Payroll-Based Journal concerns, and unresolved Plans of Correction. Do not give every item equal weight. Rank by potential harm, number of residents exposed, recurrence, and weakness of current controls.

Use the Readiness Question

For each priority, ask: What should happen? What is actually happening? How do we know? What happens when the process fails? Who verifies recovery? These questions prevent leaders from confusing policy with performance. They also turn vague anxiety into a manageable worklist.

A Better Daily Huddle

A ten-minute readiness huddle should name no more than five high-risk concerns. Each concern receives an owner, a deadline, an immediate protection if needed, and a method of verification. The DON does not need to perform every action. The DON must make accountability visible and close the loop.

Composite Field Scenario

During a Monday huddle, the team reports that the weekend was quiet. A closer review shows two hospital transfers, three missed weekly skin checks, a call-off covered by an unfamiliar agency nurse, and a family complaint about unanswered call lights. None of the items appears on the same report. The DON places them on one risk view and sees a pattern: the short-staffed evening shift did not have reliable supervisory coverage. Immediate resident follow-up is completed, but the larger action is to restore a shift-level escalation and verification process. The lesson is not that every weekend problem has one cause. It is that fragmented information can hide a common condition until a leader deliberately connects it.

What Weak Readiness Often Looks Like

The expected process is described in policy and discussed in meetings, but leaders cannot produce current resident-level evidence that it works under ordinary conditions. Audits record completion without testing resident experience, failures are corrected once without examining scope, and education is used as a substitute for redesign or competency. A useful readiness test asks the team to demonstrate practice, explain a recent failure, and show the follow-up.

A 30-Minute Team Exercise

Bring the responsible department leaders together with one real, de-identified example. Spend five minutes defining the expected process; ten minutes comparing observation, interview, and record evidence; five minutes identifying immediate resident protection and possible scope; and ten minutes assigning a system action and verification plan. End with one owner, one due time, one measure, and a scheduled recheck. If the issue suggests serious or ongoing harm, stop the exercise and activate the facility's clinical and regulatory response.

sections.title: 2. Identify the Highest-Risk Systems
sections.html:
2. Identify the Highest-Risk Systems

The loudest problem is not always the greatest risk. A missing form may be noisy; an unreliable change-in-condition process may be quiet until a resident deteriorates. Good readiness work distinguishes urgency, severity, and system reach.

Use Four Ranking Factors

Rate each concern by severity of possible harm, likelihood of occurrence, number of residents exposed, and detectability. A problem that can cause serious harm, occurs often, affects many residents, and is hard to detect deserves leadership attention even when no recent event has occurred. This is a practical risk-ranking method, not a regulatory scoring formula.

Look Beyond Nursing

Clinical outcomes depend on food and nutrition, pharmacy, rehabilitation, social services, environmental services, activities, medical providers, transportation, supplies, and administration. If a resident misses dialysis because transportation failed, the issue is not simply a nursing documentation defect. If a pressure injury worsens because equipment was unavailable, purchasing and maintenance are part of the system.

Find Concentrated Risk

Map where risk concentrates: a new unit manager, heavy agency use on weekends, several new admissions, a high-acuity hallway, late treatments on evening shift, repeated grievances from one unit, or incomplete competencies around a specialized service. Facility-wide averages can hide these pockets.

Avoid the Audit Trap

More auditing is not automatically safer. An audit that counts incomplete boxes without identifying residents at risk or why the work failed produces activity, not control. Use a small number of meaningful checks, review failures promptly, correct individual risk, and change the system that produced the failure.

Composite Field Scenario

A leadership team spends two weeks correcting unsigned refrigerator logs because the logs are easy to count. At the same time, residents returning from the hospital sometimes wait hours for reconciled orders. The missing signatures matter, but medication-transition risk has a greater potential for serious harm and affects several departments. The DON reorders the work: immediate food-safety controls remain in place, while an interdisciplinary team maps the hospital-return process, tests three recent cases, and fixes after-hours pharmacy and practitioner escalation. Risk ranking does not excuse lower-priority defects; it prevents measurable but minor work from consuming attention needed for greater exposure.

sections.title: 3. Think Like a Surveyor

3. Think Like a Surveyor

Surveyors begin with information before they enter the building. They may review prior deficiencies, complaints, facility-reported incidents, staffing data, and MDS indicators. Onsite, they do not wait for leaders to explain the building before observing residents.

Understand the Investigation Path

The current Long-Term Care Survey Process combines offsite preparation, facility entrance, initial-pool screening, sample selection, resident investigations, facility tasks, deficiency determination, and an exit conference. The practical lesson for a DON is simple: surveyors arrive with hypotheses, then test them using resident experience, observation, interviews, records, and facility systems.

Do Not Rehearse Answers

Staff should never be coached to memorize slogans or conceal uncertainty. They should understand the work, know where to find current information, describe what they personally do, and say when they need to verify something. Authentic competence is more convincing than identical scripted responses.

Test Consistency

Choose one issue and ask a resident, nurse aide, nurse, unit manager, and record the same basic question. If the stories differ, the response is not to make everyone use the same words. Determine whether the care plan is current, whether assignments communicate it, whether supplies exist, and whether supervision detects missed care.

Use Current Survey Resources

CMS Critical Element Pathways and facility-task resources reveal the evidence surveyors may explore. Use them as mirrors for operations, not as promises that checking every box prevents a citation. Always confirm the current version and pair federal materials with state law, state guidance, and facility policy.

Composite Field Scenario

The facility's internal scorecard shows ninety-eight percent completion for fall interventions. A resident tells a surveyor that the floor mat is often folded behind the recliner. The aide says the mat is used at night; the care plan says it is used whenever the resident is in bed; and the resident sleeps in the recliner. The percentage concealed a question the audit never asked. A surveyor follows the contradiction across interview, observation, and record. The DON's improved review stops asking only whether an intervention is listed and begins asking whether it fits the resident's actual routine and reaches the shift providing care.

sections.title: 4. Follow the Resident, Not the Binder

4. Follow the Resident, Not the Binder

Resident-centered tracing asks whether the entire path of care makes sense. The investigator begins with the resident and moves backward and outward: what happened, what should have happened, who knew, what was documented, and what the facility did next.

Begin With the Person

Observe the resident's condition, positioning, comfort, dignity, equipment, environment, and interactions. When appropriate, ask what matters to the resident and whether the planned care is occurring. Only then move into the record. This sequence reduces the risk of letting documentation tell you what you expect to see.

Trace the Clinical Chain

A reliable chain connects recognition, assessment, notification, orders, care planning, assignment, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation. A break anywhere can expose a resident. For example, a fall intervention may appear in a progress note yet never reach the nurse-aide assignment. A treatment may be signed as complete although the required product was unavailable.

Resolve Contradictions

Contradictions are valuable signals. If the resident says showers are often missed but assignment sheets show completion, investigate respectfully. Determine whether the preference changed, staffing interfered, documentation is inaccurate, or the resident experienced a different problem. Do not erase the contradiction by choosing the most convenient source.

End With the System

After protecting the resident, ask whether others could be affected. Review similar residents, the same shift, the same process, and the same staff competency. The difference between an isolated correction and a system correction is the deliberate search for additional exposure.

Composite Field Scenario

A wound binder contains current measurements and treatment orders, yet the resident grimaces during repositioning and says the preferred schedule is not followed after supper. The evening assignment does not include the individualized positioning approach documented in the care plan. The resident receives assessment and comfort measures, and leaders examine other residents whose interventions depend on shift assignments. The weakness is not the absence of wound information; it is the failure of information to travel from assessment to the people delivering care. The tracer makes that broken connection visible.

PART II — INVESTIGATE THE WAY CARE IS DELIVERED

5. Use Observation, Interviews, and Records Together

No single source tells the whole truth. Observation shows the present moment. Interviews reveal experience and understanding. Records show the documented clinical and operational path. Strong conclusions come from triangulating all three.

Observation

Observe ordinary work without turning the round into a performance. Watch hand hygiene, medication administration, transfers, meals, call-light response, positioning, infection precautions, equipment use, and resident interactions. Record facts: who, what, where, and when. Avoid conclusions until other evidence is reviewed.

Interview

Use open questions first: Tell me how this resident's transfer is completed. What do you do if you notice a change? How do you learn a new intervention? Residents should be approached privately and respectfully when possible. Staff should understand that uncertainty can be followed by checking a source; guessing is more dangerous than saying, 'I need to verify that.'

Record Review

Review only what answers the clinical question. Locate the assessment, care plan, orders, treatment or administration record, progress notes, provider and representative notification, and follow-up. Check dates and sequence. A late entry may be clinically useful but cannot prove that a step occurred at the required time without supporting evidence.

Triangulate Before Acting

When sources agree, confidence increases. When they differ, widen the review. A record may be complete while the resident reports missed care. An employee may describe correct technique but not use it. The purpose is not to catch someone; it is to identify the point where the system becomes unreliable.

Composite Field Scenario

A medication record indicates that an inhaler was administered. Observation shows the resident struggling with technique. The nurse explains the standard steps accurately, but the resident says no one has checked technique since admission. The care plan describes self-administration support without a recent evaluation. Each source alone offers a partial story. Together they show a need for resident assessment, immediate coaching, and a review of how the facility verifies competency when residents participate in medication use.

sections.title: 6. Conduct Effective Tracer Rounds

6. Conduct Effective Tracer Rounds

A tracer round is a short, disciplined investigation—not a complete mock survey. Its value comes from choosing the right resident, asking a focused question, correcting risk promptly, and returning later to see whether the correction lasted.

Choose Intentionally

Rotate among new admissions, residents with recent significant change, hospital returns, high-risk medications, wounds, falls, weight loss, dialysis, behavioral symptoms, restraints or restrictive practices, infections, hospice, and grievances. Include nights and weekends. Random selection has value, but risk-based selection finds more important weaknesses.

Keep the Scope Manageable

A useful tracer can take twenty to forty minutes. Define the question, review the care at the bedside, interview one or two people, inspect the minimum relevant record, and determine the next action. When a serious or systemic concern appears, convert the tracer into a formal investigation with appropriate leadership support.

Correct Without Contaminating

Protect the resident immediately, but preserve accurate information needed to understand what happened. Do not backdate, recreate evidence, coach accounts, or quietly replace missing documentation. Record the gap, complete current clinical work, notify as required, and investigate the cause.

Close the Loop

Every finding needs one of four dispositions: no concern found; isolated issue corrected and verified; possible system issue expanded; or urgent concern escalated. A long list of findings without disposition becomes another source of organizational risk.

Composite Field Scenario

A manager attempts to trace twenty residents in one afternoon and produces a long list of small defects without clear follow-up. The DON changes the method. The next tracer focuses on one new admission with an anticoagulant, reviewing reconciliation, monitoring, resident education, and communication to direct-care staff. A missing laboratory follow-up is corrected immediately, three similar admissions are screened, and the after-hours tracking process is redesigned. One focused tracer produces more protection than an unfocused sweep because it reaches disposition and verification.

7. Prepare Staff for Surveyor Interviews

The goal is not to create perfect speakers. The goal is to create staff who understand their work, can describe how they protect residents, and know how to get help when a situation falls outside their role.

Teach the Work, Then Practice the Conversation

Start with competency: abuse prevention and reporting, changes in condition, resident rights, infection prevention, emergency procedures, care-plan access, assignment communication, and role-specific high-risk skills. Then use brief practice interviews during normal rounds. Ask staff to explain their process in their own words.

Four Safe Interview Habits

Listen to the entire question. Answer what is known from personal practice. Do not guess or offer unrelated information. If a policy, order, or assignment must be checked, say so and retrieve it. Staff should never be instructed to delay, misdirect, or avoid a surveyor.

Respond to a Knowledge Gap

A missed answer is a supervision signal. Protect any affected resident, reteach the correct process, verify competency, determine whether others share the gap, and document the response. Punishing embarrassment teaches concealment. Calm correction builds reliability.

Prepare All Shifts

Survey readiness fails when education reaches only daytime staff. Include night shift, weekend staff, agency personnel, new hires, dietary employees, environmental services, therapy, activities, social services, and department heads. Match questions to each person's actual role.

Composite Field Scenario

A nurse aide freezes when asked how to report suspected neglect, even though annual education is documented. The supervisor initially wants to provide the correct words and move on. Instead, the DON protects the learning environment, asks the aide to show the reporting resources, verifies understanding, and samples other shifts. Several employees know to tell a supervisor but do not understand the immediate reporting route if that supervisor is unavailable. The response becomes a competency and escalation fix—not a rehearsal of a model answer.

8. Strengthen High-Risk Clinical Systems

Survey exposure concentrates where care is complex, time-sensitive, or dependent on several handoffs. The safest approach is to define the clinical chain and test the connections, not merely count completed forms.

Changes in Condition

Test whether staff recognize change, obtain an appropriate assessment, notify the practitioner and representative as required, carry out orders, update the care plan, monitor response, and escalate when the resident does not improve. Review after-hours reliability and access to practitioners.

Falls, Skin, Nutrition, and Infection

For each system, connect risk identification to individualized intervention and evaluation. A generic intervention applied to every resident is weak. Verify that direct-care staff know the current approach, equipment is present, refusals are addressed, and trends lead to revised plans.

Review high-risk medications, unnecessary-drug concerns, monitoring, gradual dose reduction where applicable, pharmacy recommendations, storage, labeling, controlled substances, and administration practice. 9. Recognize Immediate-Jeopardy Warning Signs

Immediate jeopardy is a regulatory determination, not a label a facility assigns to itself. Leaders still need to recognize situations that may involve serious harm or a likelihood of serious harm and respond without delay.

Think in Terms of Serious Harm and Continuing Exposure

Warning signs include unaddressed abuse or neglect allegations, failure to protect after an allegation, elopement with serious risk, severe medication or treatment failures, widespread infection-control breakdown, inability to provide essential care, dangerous equipment, and delayed response to acute deterioration. Context matters; no checklist replaces current Appendix Q guidance and professional judgment.

Protect First

Stop ongoing exposure. Obtain emergency assessment and treatment. Separate an alleged perpetrator from residents when indicated. Secure unsafe equipment or supplies. Provide additional supervision. PART III — CORRECT THE SYSTEM, NOT THE PAPER

10. Correct Problems Immediately and Systemically

The first correction protects the resident. The second correction protects other residents. The third correction changes the process. The fourth proves the new process works. Skipping any level leaves the facility vulnerable.

Four Levels of Correction

Resident correction addresses the person affected. Scope review identifies others who may be exposed. System correction changes the conditions that allowed failure. Verification determines whether actions were implemented and effective. These levels help leaders avoid mistaking a completed task for a corrected system.

Separate Containment From Improvement

Containment may include assessment, notification, equipment replacement, staffing adjustment, or direct supervision. Longer-term improvement may require workflow redesign, clearer accountability, competency validation, supply controls, or information-system changes. Both matter, but they operate on different timelines.

Assign Owners With Authority

The person named as owner must be able to obtain resources, direct work, and report barriers. 'Nursing' is not an owner. A unit manager, staff-development nurse, infection preventionist, dietary manager, administrator, or corporate partner can own a defined action. The DON remains accountable for clinical leadership without becoming the doer of every task.

Whenever practical, the person who verifies effectiveness should be different from the person who completed the correction. Verification should sample varied shifts and conditions. A process that works only when leaders are watching is not yet reliable.

A resident's pressure-relief cushion is missing. Staff locate a replacement, and the immediate problem appears solved. 11. Find the Root Cause Behind Repeat Deficiencies

A repeat deficiency is often evidence that the prior response treated a visible symptom. Root-cause work asks why the expected process failed under real conditions and why ordinary controls did not detect or correct it.

Describe the Problem Precisely

Use a statement with who or what was affected, the expected process, the actual deviation, timing, location, and consequence or risk. 'Staff need more education' is not a problem statement. 'Evening-shift treatment records were signed before supplies were available for four residents over six days' can be investigated.

Use More Than Five Whys

Repeated why-questions can help, but they become shallow when leaders stop at 'staff forgot.' Examine workflow, workload, handoffs, access to information, competency, equipment, scheduling, supervision, incentives, and measurement. Ask what made the wrong action easier than the right one.

Distinguish Active Error From Latent Conditions

An employee may miss a step, but the system may also have unclear assignments, competing tasks, missing supplies, confusing screens, weak orientation, or no escalation route. Accountability still matters. Root-cause analysis improves fairness by connecting individual conduct to the conditions leaders control.

12. Write a Credible Plan of Correction

A Plan of Correction is both a regulatory response and an operational commitment. The strongest plan is specific enough to execute, broad enough to address the system, and measurable enough to verify.

Answer the Required Questions

For each deficiency, describe how the affected resident was corrected when possible; how other potentially affected residents were identified; what systemic changes will prevent recurrence; how performance will be monitored; and the completion date. Follow the instructions from the applicable survey agency and current CMS guidance.

Avoid Empty Language

Phrases such as 'staff were reeducated,' 'will continue to monitor,' or 'all residents have the potential to be affected' are incomplete without who, what, when, scope, measure, threshold, response to failure, and responsible role. Training may be part of an action, but it rarely changes a poorly designed process by itself.

Make Dates Honest

A completion date should represent the point at which required correction is implemented, not the date when leaders hope to begin. Monitoring may continue beyond that date. Do not backdate activity or describe planned actions as completed.

The Administrator, DON, department owners, and corporate partners should understand the same plan. Audit tools, education, revised policies, assignments, and QAPI oversight must agree with the written submission. 13. Create Evidence That Corrections Are Working

Evidence is not a pile of paper. It is a traceable demonstration that an action occurred, reached the intended people or process, and produced a safer, more reliable result.

Match Evidence to the Claim

If the claim is that staff are competent, attendance sheets are insufficient; use observation or return demonstration. If the claim is that care-plan interventions reach the bedside, review assignments and observe care. If the claim is that a new escalation path works, sample actual events and response times.

Create an Evidence Index

For each corrective action, record the deficiency or risk, required evidence, location, responsible custodian, date range, review status, and any confidentiality restrictions. Use controlled storage. Do not create parallel clinical records or unsecured collections of protected health information.

Preserve Integrity

Evidence must be contemporaneous, accurate, and attributable. Never alter timestamps, recreate signatures, backfill audits, or ask employees to produce a preferred account. When a record is missing or late, address that fact transparently and follow current policy for corrections or late entries.

A useful evidence set connects baseline, action, implementation, outcome, failure response, and sustained performance. Leaders should be able to explain what changed and show representative proof without handing over an uncontrolled mass of documents.

14. Test Whether Improvements Are Durable

A correction that survives only the first week is not a reliable correction. Durability means the expected process continues after attention fades, leaders rotate, census changes, and difficult shifts occur.

Design the Monitoring Plan

Define the measure, population, sample, frequency, responsible reviewer, passing threshold, duration, and response to failure. Sample nights, weekends, new employees, agency staff, high-acuity units, and unusual conditions when relevant. A convenient sample can produce false confidence.

Use Leading and Lagging Measures

Leading measures test whether the process occurs, such as timely assessments or intervention communication. Lagging measures show outcomes, such as injuries or avoidable transfers. Add a balancing measure when improvement could create a new problem—for example, reducing agency hours while watching overtime, missed care, turnover, and resident outcomes.

Respond to Failure

A failed audit is not simply added to the next month's denominator. Protect residents, determine cause, correct the process, and decide whether the monitoring plan should reset or expand. Repeated failure despite action requires leadership escalation and possibly a different intervention.

Do not close an improvement because the team is tired of reviewing it. Close or step down monitoring when performance meets the defined threshold for the planned duration, no concerning balancing trend exists, and the process has transferred to routine operational oversight.

15. Use QAPI to Support Survey Readiness

QAPI is not the place where problems go to become meeting minutes. It is the facility's structured method for learning from data, improving systems, and sustaining performance.

Connect Daily Control and Formal Improvement

Not every missed task needs a Performance Improvement Project. Daily management should correct isolated variation. QAPI should focus on high-risk, high-volume, or problem-prone systems; adverse trends; repeat deficiencies; and issues that require interdisciplinary redesign.

Use the Five Elements

CMS describes five elements of QAPI: design and scope; governance and leadership; feedback, data systems, and monitoring; performance improvement projects; and systematic analysis and systemic action. The DON should be able to show how a selected project fits these elements and changes care.

Choose a Useful Aim

A useful aim names the population, outcome or process, baseline, target, and timeframe. 'Improve falls' is too vague. An aim might reduce repeat falls among a defined population while preserving mobility and monitoring injury severity, restraint use, and therapy access.

The Quality Assessment and Assurance committee should receive clear information about risk, corrective actions, results, barriers, and resource needs. Confidentiality protections and applicable regulations must be respected. The committee's value is demonstrated by decisions and sustained improvement, not by the thickness of its minutes.

One project addresses avoidable transfer risk using response-time, assessment-completion, transfer, and staff-burden measures. Small tests reveal an after-hours practitioner-access problem that requires an administrative contract decision. PART V — LEAD THE SURVEY WITH CONTROL

16. Build the Survey Command Center

A survey command center should make requests, responsibilities, resident risks, and communications visible without disrupting care. Its purpose is coordination—not controlling surveyors or manufacturing documents.

Assign Roles Before Entrance

Name an executive lead, clinical lead, survey liaison, request-log coordinator, document runner, staffing contact, IT support, and unit coverage plan. Small facilities can combine roles, but responsibilities must remain clear. Identify backups for every essential role.

Prepare Current Materials

Maintain an entrance-ready index aligned with current federal and state requests. Confirm who can produce census and matrix information, staffing records, policies, incident logs, QAPI materials, infection-control information, contracts, and other requested records. The index is useful only when the underlying information is accurate and accessible.

Control Requests

Log the exact request, surveyor, time received, owner, due time, status, and time delivered. Clarify ambiguous requests respectfully. Provide what was requested through the designated process. Do not alter records or overwhelm the team with irrelevant material.

Protect Resident Care

Survey response should not pull essential leaders and staff away from resident needs. Arrange relief for interviews, preserve medication and treatment coverage, and monitor clinical operations throughout the survey. A calm command center keeps the facility functioning while supporting transparent access.

17. Lead the First Hour of Survey

The first hour reveals whether the facility has a functioning system. Surveyors begin observing quickly. Leaders should be welcoming, accurate, organized, and focused on residents—not consumed by appearances.

Receive and Notify

Confirm identification according to facility procedure, notify the Administrator and designated leaders, provide requested workspace, and begin the entrance process. Do not create a facility-wide panic message. Use a factual notification that activates roles and preserves normal care.

Deliver Required Information

The survey team coordinator will identify information needed immediately and during the entrance conference. Use the current entrance materials and respond within stated timeframes. If information is unavailable, report the status honestly, identify the owner, and give a realistic update.

18. Manage Requests, Interviews, and Documentation

During survey, small coordination failures can create confusion: duplicate requests, incomplete copies, contradictory responses, missing follow-up, or leaders who do not know where a document went. A disciplined process protects accuracy.

Use One Request Log

All requests should enter a single visible queue. Record exact wording and deadlines. The coordinator should avoid interpreting the request beyond what was asked. Sensitive information must be handled according to law and facility policy.

Support Interviews Appropriately

Arrange coverage and a suitable location when requested. Staff and residents must be able to speak freely. A facility representative should attend only when permitted or requested. After an interview, do not interrogate the participant about what was said.

Correct New Risk Immediately

If a surveyor identifies or the facility discovers an active care concern, assess and protect the resident immediately. Notify the appropriate practitioner, representative, leadership, or agency as required. Correction does not erase a potential deficiency, but delay can increase harm.

Maintain a Decision Record

Keep a concise chronology of significant requests, clinical actions, leadership decisions, and communications. Separate factual notes from legal analysis or privileged advice. Use qualified counsel or compliance resources when needed.

19. Respond Professionally to Findings

Survey discussions can feel personal, especially when leaders believe context is missing. The DON's task is to protect residents, understand the evidence, and communicate facts without defensiveness or speculation.

Listen for the Elements

Ask what requirement or concern is being examined, which resident or process is involved, what evidence is missing, and whether additional factual information would be useful. Take careful notes. Do not argue in hallways or pressure staff to change statements.

Provide Relevant Evidence

If the facility has contemporaneous information that directly addresses the concern, organize and provide it through the designated process. Explain context concisely. More paper does not strengthen a weak response; relevance and integrity do.

Correct While the Survey Continues

Begin appropriate correction when a concern is credible, regardless of whether the final citation is known. Expand the review when others may be affected. Keep the survey team informed as appropriate without representing preliminary action as proof of full correction.

Use the Exit Conference Wisely

The exit conference is a time to understand preliminary findings and clarify factual inaccuracies, not to litigate every disagreement. Record the information needed for follow-up. Afterward, debrief the team, protect confidentiality, preserve documents, and prepare for the formal process.

A surveyor raises concern about delayed practitioner notification. A manager immediately argues that the resident was stable. sections.html:
20. Maintain Year-Round Survey Readiness

The end of survey should not be the end of readiness. A sustainable system distributes ownership, uses a predictable cadence, and makes improvement part of ordinary management.

Daily, Weekly, Monthly, Quarterly

Daily work identifies urgent risk and closes loops. Weekly work reviews trends, tracers, staffing, and open corrections. Monthly work tests high-risk systems and reports measures. Quarterly work uses QAA/QAPI governance to examine patterns, resources, facility assessment implications, and durability.

Distribute Ownership

Department heads and unit leaders should own defined readiness systems. The DON coordinates clinical risk but cannot personally manage every audit, competency, request, and corrective action. Build role clarity, backup coverage, and escalation expectations.

Refresh the Risk Profile

Resident population, services, staffing, equipment, and external requirements change. Update readiness priorities after significant events, new services, leadership turnover, regulatory changes, or adverse trends. Align the facility assessment, staffing competencies, emergency planning, and QAPI priorities.

Measure the Culture

A survey-ready culture reports concerns early, protects residents before protecting reputation, treats documentation as a clinical tool, and learns from failure. Leaders reinforce that culture through their response to bad news. If employees are punished for surfacing risk, the building becomes less visible and less safe.

Two months after survey, audits have stopped and the same few leaders again carry every open action. The DON converts the Plan of Correction calendar into routine management: daily risk huddles, weekly tracer review, monthly system tests, and quarterly QAPI decisions. About the Author

Averose Pastores is a Director of Nursing and long-term-care nursing leader with firsthand experience navigating the clinical, operational, staffing, regulatory, and human demands of the role. Her work focuses on helping nursing leaders replace crisis-driven management with practical systems that protect residents, strengthen staff accountability, and make improvement sustainable. She is also the author of The New DON's First 90 Days, Book One in The Practical DON Leadership Series.
